# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

```{python}
#| include: false
import _helpers as H

bS, gB, gW = H.head("beta_S"), H.head("gamma_B"), H.head("gamma_W")
kA, nA = H.rob_count("A", "beta_S", "excludes_zero")
sAll, nAll = H.rob_count("all", "beta_S", "keeps_sign")
sec_k = H.SEC.get("multiplicity", {}).get("n_bh_reject")
sec_n = H.SEC.get("multiplicity", {}).get("n_family")
```

We asked whether scheduled national elections are associated with deterioration in the cyclically adjusted primary balance of EU member states, and whether the association varies with population ageing. We answered with a pre-registered design that was frozen, hashed and made public before any outcome was related to an election variable, and we reported every robustness specification that was run.

The main finding is modest and should be stated with its limits. A full year of pre-election exposure to a scheduled election is associated with a CAPB lower by `{python} H.num(-bS.get("estimate"), 2)` pp of potential GDP (95% interval `{python} H.ival(bS.get("ci_lo"), bS.get("ci_hi"))`; Holm-adjusted $p$ = `{python} H.pval(bS.get("p_holm"), 3)`). The headline is `{python} H.evidence_core()`. `{python} H.evidence_limits()` We therefore describe the evidence as weak and fragile, not as established, and not as a causal effect of elections. <!-- CHECKED-STATIC (2026-10-14 against robustness.json; re-check only if the suite is re-run) -->

In the headline we find no evidence that the association varies with a country's average level of ageing at a magnitude that matters: the interval for $\gamma_B$ (`{python} H.ival(gB.get("ci_lo"), gB.get("ci_hi"))`) lies within the pre-registered band of ±`{python} H.num(H.sesoi(), 1)` pp per standard deviation, but not in the inference sensitivities, and it is a cross-country contrast and not a statement about ageing itself. Exploratory analyses of moderation by fiscal-rule strength, nonlinear ageing, debt, accession cohort and euro membership find nothing that survives multiplicity adjustment, with intervals too wide to detect heterogeneity of a relevant size (@sec-exploratory). The within-country component, `{python} H.ival(gW.get("ci_lo"), gW.get("ci_hi"))`, is uninformative. Among ten secondary outcomes, `{python} H.cnt(sec_k, sec_n)` survives multiplicity adjustment (the change in the CAPB, which is arithmetically related to the level and is not independent corroboration), and no spending or revenue component accounts clearly for the CAPB association. In the separate predictive module, no model of the next-year change in the CAPB is distinguishable from persistence, and the political and demographic block adds nothing to prediction; this neither supports nor contradicts the association (@sec-predictive).

Three implications follow. For research on political budget cycles, the exercise illustrates how much of the statistical support for a small, imprecise association depends on estimator and inference choices, and why pre-registration, equivalence reading and full reporting of specifications are useful in this literature. For policy, the evidence is too weak, too imprecise and too conditional on a model-based, revised indicator to support a claim that elections cause fiscal loosening in the EU, or that ageing changes this. For future work, three extensions would increase learning most: a real-time or vintage-aware outcome, to address the revision problem (the mean absolute revision of `{python} H.fact("revision")` pp is of the same order as the estimated association and the SESOI, [Appendix E](#sec-app-revisions)); a design with more precision on the within-country ageing component, which would need more elections or a more direct measure of electoral age composition; and heterogeneity-robust estimators for recurring exposures.

Everything in the results chapters is generated from committed result files, and the pipeline from hashed raw inputs to the frozen extract and the results is documented in [Appendix D](#sec-app-repro).
